archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (finishing slump)
archetype.definition: Columbus is breaking even on shot attempts and getting league-average goaltending, but its goal differential is being dragged down by the league's worst shooting percentage. Its chance quality is below average, though, so a correction lifts it toward mediocrity rather than the playoffs.

report.headline: Even possession, league-worst finishing: Columbus is better than 7-11, not good enough
report.take:
Columbus came into 2026-27 off its best two seasons in this window: 89 points, then 92, with a 0.52 xGF % last year. Eighteen games in, the Blue Jackets are 7-11-0, last in the Metropolitan, 27th on the site, and on a 64-point pace. The 2.5 goals a game they score ranks 29th, and a -13 differential has them 25th in Goal Diff / GP. On its face, that is a team sliding back toward the 2022-24 bottom-feeders.

The underlying play says something less dramatic. The 5-on-5 CF % is exactly 0.5, 12th in the league. Shots on goal are 27.1 a game against 27.6 allowed, both mid-pack. Goalies GSAx is +2.2, 14th. What is missing is finishing. The skaters are shooting 8.8% in all situations, 32nd of 32 and well under the league's 11.4%. That single number explains most of why a roughly even-shot team carries a 97.9 all-situations PDO and a goal differential this ugly. Kent Johnson (8 goals, 18 points) is the only forward finishing at a normal clip. Adam Fantilli has 5 goals on 53 shots, Sean Monahan 1 in 17 games, and Conor Garland none in 15.

Where the numbers don't flatter them is shot quality. An xGF % of 0.483 ranks 23rd and is a clear step down from last season's 0.52. Columbus holds the puck about as much as its opponents but generates slightly worse looks with it, so some of the cold shooting is earned rather than pure bad luck. Special teams are a real hole on both sides, with the PP at 18.2% (26th) and the PK at 73.5% (23rd). The forward group grades a D, and the blueline's C is propped up by Zach Werenski's 27.96 minutes and +6 while Erik Gudbranson sits at -10. In net, the split is the story. Cam Talbot is at .909 with +5.4 GSAx, while Jet Greaves is at .875 and -3.4, and Greaves has the larger share of the starts.

The direction is the worry. Columbus is 1-4 over its last five, scoring 1.8 a game, and most of the wins in the last ten needed overtime. Shooting this cold almost always thaws, and when it does this looks like a sub-.500 team that scores closer to league average, not a 64-point one. The hole is already deep in a division where Carolina and New Jersey are running away, and the shot-quality slippage from last year means the bounce-back has a ceiling.

strengths.title: Possession is genuinely even
strengths.body: A 0.5 CF % (12th) and shot volume close to the league average on both ends mean Columbus is not being territorially outplayed. That base is what makes the record look worse than the team. It also matches last season's 0.51, so it is a stable trait rather than an 18-game blip.

strengths.title: Talbot has been the real starter
strengths.body: Cam Talbot's .909 and +5.4 GSAx rank him 17th of 71 goalies. He is the reason team GSAx sits above the league average despite Greaves' struggles. If the crease tilts further toward Talbot, the goals-against side should hold up.

strengths.title: Johnson and Werenski driving production
strengths.body: Kent Johnson leads the team with 18 points and is the one forward converting at a normal rate. Werenski, 21st of 259 on the defense tab, logs nearly 28 minutes with 15 points and a +6 on a team that is underwater. Both look sustainable; the problem is how little support they get.

concerns.title: League-worst finishing, partly earned
concerns.body: An 8.8% shooting rate, last in the league and far below its average, has sunk the offense to 30th. Pure luck at that extreme usually corrects. But the 0.483 xGF % says Columbus is generating below-average chances, so expect a rise toward average, not a surge past it.

concerns.title: Special teams bleeding on both ends
concerns.body: The power play converts 18.2% (26th) and the penalty kill holds 73.5% (23rd), each about four points worse than the league average. History says the PP has never been good here, with no season in this window above 19.5%. That half is unlikely to fix itself.

concerns.title: Shot quality slipped from last year
concerns.body: Last season's 0.52 xGF % backed a 92-point team. This year's 0.483 is a real step back, with forward depth the weak link: a D forward grade, Monahan at 0.426 and Garland at 0.42. This is the part of the decline that is not noise.

trend.note: October's 5-7 at least held a near-even run of results into late in the month. The last five games have gone 1-4 with only 1.8 goals a game, and the offense has gotten colder rather than starting to correct.

weekAhead.headline: Four road games: two winnable, two against stronger teams
weekAhead.body:
Columbus spends the whole week away, with a mixed slate. Chicago is the softest opponent in the league by almost every measure: 31st on the site, last in Goal Diff / GP, a 0.409 xGF %, and a .873 save %. Toronto is 25th on the site but has a 26.7% power play that lines up badly against the Columbus kill. The bookends are harder. The Islanders' A-graded goaltending (+11.9 GSAx, 3rd) is exactly the wrong matchup for a team that can't finish. New Jersey's 0.56 CF % and 21.8 shots allowed a game threaten the one thing Columbus does well, possession.

The realistic target is beating Chicago, splitting the Toronto and Islanders games, and taking whatever comes in New Jersey. The Islanders win on goaltending more than play: a 0.48 CF %, 28.8 shots allowed a game and a 102.3 PDO. Columbus can tilt the ice there, but it needs pucks to go in.

keyMatchups.title: Chicago is the slump-breaker
keyMatchups.body: Chicago's defense allows 8 points a game to forwards, 1.48 above expectation and 31st in the league. Its goalies sit at -10.3 GSAx. If the Columbus shooting percentage is going to turn anywhere this week, it is here.

keyMatchups.title: Columbus PK against Toronto's power play
keyMatchups.body: Toronto converts 26.7% on the power play, 6th in the league, against a Columbus kill at 73.5%. Toronto's 5-on-5 play is weak, with a 0.461 xGF %, so staying out of the box is the clearest path to points.

keyMatchups.title: Islanders and Devils goaltending versus volume
keyMatchups.body: The Islanders' .911 save % ranks 3rd, a wall for a team shooting 8.8%. New Jersey is the opposite case. Its 66% penalty kill is 30th in the league, giving even this weak power play a real opening if Columbus can draw penalties.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in net. Talbot's +5.4 GSAx against Greaves' -3.4 is the biggest controllable edge Columbus has across four road games.

restOfSeason.body:
With 64 games left, the shooting percentage is the variable most likely to move. It cannot stay last in the league at this gap to average for a team with even possession, and a rise toward normal turns a 2.5-goal offense into something closer to league-average scoring. Against that, the 0.483 xGF %, the weak special teams and the shallow forward group are structural. I expect Columbus to play close to .500 hockey the rest of the way, landing around 70-80 standings points. That is a clear improvement on the 64-point pace, but well short of last year's 92 and of a playoff spot in a Metropolitan led by Carolina and New Jersey.

The sustainable pieces are possession, Werenski, Johnson and Talbot. The pieces likely to improve are team finishing and a few forwards, Fantilli and Monahan above all. The piece that probably doesn't improve without changes is the special teams, which have been below average in every season in this window.

projections.stat: Goals scored / game, rest of season

swingFactors: Team shooting % returning toward league average
Talbot getting the bulk of the starts
Penalty kill climbing out of the bottom third

confidence.note: An 18-game sample with an extreme shooting % gives a clear direction; the size of the correction is the uncertain part.
